title: The 5 Paradoxes Every Leader Must Learn to Live With
author: The Good Boss newsletter
summary: This Good Boss essay frames leadership not as a set of problems to be solved but as a standing set of tensions to be inhabited, arguing that the most effective leaders stop trying to resolve five recurring paradoxes and instead learn to hold both sides at once. The Control Paradox names the trap in which a leader, accountable for outcomes but unable to do the work, tightens their grip and inadvertently trains the team into passivity. The Competence Paradox describes the painful transition for high performers promoted out of doing and into enabling, where jumping in to fix things quietly robs the team of the chance to grow. The Clarity Paradox holds that leaders must supply direction while living in genuine ambiguity, so being clear cannot mean being certain; the Trust Paradox insists that trust is earned by extending it first; and the Ego Paradox warns that the spotlight of authority tempts leaders to center themselves precisely when the job is to make others shine. The piece closes by reframing these tensions as permanent features of the role that reward embrace rather than resistance.
points: The Control Paradox is a self-reinforcing loop: a leader who bridges their accountability gap by reviewing drafts and rewriting work signals distrust, the team stops taking initiative, and the leader responds by tightening the grip further — so the remedy is clear expectations and a high bar while letting the team own the 'how'.

The Competence Paradox stings high performers most: the very skill that earned the promotion (doing) must now be withheld, because every time a manager jumps in to fix things the team loses a chance to build the competence it needs to run without them.

The Clarity Paradox reframes what leaders owe their teams: clarity is not certainty, and the honest posture is 'here's what we know, here's what we don't, and here's what we'll try' rather than faked confidence or delayed decisions.

The Trust Paradox reverses the usual order — leaders must extend real ownership, public backing, and genuine listening before the team has 'proven' itself, because trust is earned by going first, not demanded through rules and reminders.

The Ego Paradox identifies the subtlest failure mode: authority makes a leader's presence and opinions carry disproportionate weight, which tempts them to take credit and hold the final say, whereas the best leaders make themselves almost invisible so others can shine.
quotes: So what do great leaders do? They make expectations clear, they hold the bar high, and they let their team own the “how”.
Every time you “jump in” to help your team, your team loses the chance to learn and grow.
Letting go of doing doesn’t mean letting go of standards. It means raising others to meet them.
But you don’t really have those answers - all you have is the gray and the murky. You never have the ‘full’ data, or the ‘perfect’ formula.
But you can’t force trust with rules and reminders. The only way to gain trust is to earn it.
The best leaders I have met have conquered their ego, and that’s exactly what makes them great.
